<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A executed the comparative and pressure-testing work more decisively. A's central move — that authorized categories (minefields, BVR missiles) already sever real-time human choice of victim, and that "defensive" interceptors already make lethal target-identification calls — put real pressure on B's core accountability/judgment distinction, and B's rebuttal (reflex vs. judgment) was itself punctured by A's airliner/spoofing point in A4.3, which B's closing never answered. B's sharpest moment was exposing the tension between A's "invisible to inspectors" and "logged/reviewable" claims, but A's distinction between external verification and internal command accountability blunted it without a further B response. Most decisively, A's pressure question about civilian-death tradeoffs forced B into an explicit "control over lives" position that A's closing weaponized cleanly, while B's closing pivoted away rather than reframing or softening that concession. This made A's case easier to vote for on the stakes that matter most to the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's own "would you still ban it if it saved civilian lives" concession (B4.4), turned into the decisive weighing point in A's closing, while B's closing failed to recontextualize or rebut that framing.</best_rebuttal>
